speaker: RJ Scaringe
title: How to build a $16B car company with RJ Scaringe, founder of Rivian
question: In the automotive industry, why do legacy automakers struggle so much to transition to a consolidated, software-defined vehicle architecture?
guest: Designing real-time operating systems and a compute platform across the vehicle are things that car companies don't historically do very well. As an industry, there's this massive supplier base of tier ones that provide functions and computers alongside them. You buy a seat, it historically comes with a little computer. You buy power windows, it has a power window computer. With the exception of two companies, every car on the road has anywhere from 50 to 150 little computers that run the car. They're all little islands of software written by suppliers on little ECUs. You can't make updates to them. None of them are written by yourself, and there are so many abstraction layers between the actual code and the manufacturer. That must go away to be competitive in a world of AI where you want deep contextual understanding across the vehicle. So every car company either tries to develop it themselves, which is hard because they don't typically have those skill sets, or tries to source it from suppliers, which is very hard because those companies are precisely the ones that don't want to see all their little computers go away.

points.core: Legacy vehicles run on dozens of separate supplier-built electronic control units.
points.note: Accept: 50 to 150 ECUs, separate microcontrollers per subsystem (seats, windows, etc.), or fragmented hardware controllers from Tier-1 vendors. Do not credit: generic claims that legacy cars have outdated tech or bad software.

points.core: Multiple supplier abstraction layers prevent automakers from cleanly updating vehicle-wide software.
points.note: Accept: isolated software islands, black-box supplier firmware, or inability to push unified over-the-air updates across subsystems. Do not credit: vague mentions of legacy tech debt without linking it to supplier code boundaries.

points.core: Legacy automakers typically lack internal software talent to build consolidated platforms.
points.note: Accept: missing in-house real-time OS or embedded software engineering capabilities because OEMs historically acted as integrators. Do not credit: generic statements about slow corporate culture or bureaucracy.

points.core: Tier-one suppliers resist consolidated architectures because consolidation cannibalizes their controller sales.
points.note: Accept: structural incentive misalignment where incumbent suppliers avoid zonal consolidation that eliminates their individual ECU hardware revenue. Do not credit: generic claims that suppliers are slow or hard to negotiate with.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Legacy automakers struggle mainly because their vehicles, organizations, and supply chains were all built around a distributed, hardware-first model that is hard to unwind.

A traditional car has 100 or more electronic control units, each bought from a different supplier with its own embedded software. The automaker acts as an integrator and often doesn't own or even see the code. Consolidating that into a few central computers means rewriting or renegotiating software that suppliers control, and those suppliers have little incentive to give up that business.

The organizations mirror the architecture. Departments are split by component (powertrain, chassis, infotainment), with budgets and processes built around multi-year hardware cycles and a fixed start of production, not continuous software releases. Software talent is scarce, and pay and culture struggle to compete with tech firms.

They also have to keep legacy platforms and dozens of model variants running profitably while funding the new architecture, so they tend to stack new systems on old ones rather than start clean. Safety certification and cybersecurity rules add further drag.

Tesla and Rivian started clean; Volkswagen's Cariad troubles show how hard retrofitting is.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Legacy automakers struggle to adopt consolidated, software-defined vehicle architectures because their supply chains, organizations, and cultures were built around distributed hardware integration rather than vertical software engineering. For decades, automakers outsourced up to a hundred specialized electronic control units per car to Tier 1 suppliers, buying bundled hardware and proprietary black-box code. Replacing that patchwork with a few central and zonal computers requires writing unified operating software and hardware abstractions that incumbents historically neither owned nor controlled, while untangling entrenched supplier contracts.

Internally, legacy firms reflect Conway’s Law: engineering teams are siloed by physical domains like powertrain, chassis, and infotainment, operating on rigid multi-year model cycles that clash with continuous software iteration, while traditional manufacturing hierarchies struggle to attract and empower top software talent. Unlike clean-sheet entrants, incumbents must execute this complex, safety-critical overhaul while simultaneously funding electrification, maintaining legacy platforms, and navigating franchised dealers whose service revenues are threatened by over-the-air updates.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Legacy automakers struggle mainly because their whole operating model was built around distributed hardware, not software. For decades, every new feature meant another electronic control unit (ECU) bought from a Tier-1 supplier such as Bosch or Continental. Each ECU came with its own closed firmware, so premium cars ended up with 100 or more ECUs from dozens of vendors. Consolidating them into a few central computers means taking that software in-house. That breaks long-standing supplier contracts, and the automaker then has to own integration, validation and liability that suppliers used to carry.

Organization is the second problem. Engineering is split into domain silos, such as powertrain, body and infotainment, each with its own budget and wiring. Development runs on five-to-seven-year hardware cycles rather than continuous software releases.

Talent and culture make it harder. Automakers compete with tech firms for software engineers and often pay less. Safety-critical validation habits also clash with fast iteration.

Legacy also brings constraints that newcomers like Tesla never had. Existing factories, dealer networks, profitable combustion-engine programs and many vehicle variants have to be supported at once.

The results show it. Volkswagen's Cariad ran into delays and ended up partnering with Rivian, and other automakers have pushed back their software platforms.

Legacy automakers struggle because their organizations, supply chains, and vehicles were built around a fragmented, hardware-first model. Traditional cars rely on dozens of specialized electronic control units (ECUs) supplied by different Tier-1 vendors, each bundling proprietary, black-box software with specific hardware. Consolidating these into a few centralized computers requires untangling decades of supplier contracts, intellectual property boundaries, and tightly coupled legacy code.

Internally, Conway’s Law works against them: engineering divisions are siloed by physical domain—such as powertrain, chassis, and infotainment—mirroring the distributed ECU layout and creating fierce organizational resistance to unified software platforms. Their cultures and waterfall development processes are optimized for multi-year hardware validation and strict functional safety compliance, clashing with the agile, continuous software integration needed for over-the-air updates. Finally, unlike clean-sheet EV startups, legacy manufacturers must fund this costly transformation and compete for top software talent while simultaneously supporting dozens of existing combustion and hybrid vehicle platforms.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Legacy automakers have to redesign the car’s electronics and the way they build cars at the same time. In a traditional vehicle, functions such as braking, climate control, and infotainment run on separate electronic control units, often bought from different suppliers with proprietary software and interfaces. Moving many of those functions onto shared computers means untangling years of dependencies, gaining more control over the software, and making sure a fault or update in one function can’t compromise another. Safety-critical functions still have to meet strict timing and reliability requirements.

The organizational shift is just as hard. Automakers have historically divided work by component and timed development around model launches. A shared software platform requires teams to coordinate across components, reuse software across models, and maintain it for years after sale. Meanwhile, the company still has to ship and service vehicles built on older architectures. That overlap makes the transition expensive before the savings from simpler wiring, fewer controllers, and reusable software can materialize.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra

Legacy automakers spent decades adding features one at a time, often buying each as a package of hardware and software from a different supplier. A vehicle can therefore have dozens of control units, each with its own interfaces, release schedule, and supplier contract. Moving their functions onto a few shared computers requires redesigning how those functions communicate, how faults are contained, and how software can be updated without compromising safety or timing.

The organizational shift is just as hard. Teams and purchasing processes built around individual components must now make decisions together about a software platform that spans the vehicle. Suppliers may own code the automaker needs to change. And the transition has to happen while existing models stay in production and vehicles already on the road remain supported. A newcomer can design around one architecture from the start. An incumbent has to build the new one while sustaining the old.
